crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Finding collaborators in grant proposals and funding means identifying researchers whose expertise, data, or institutional role can strengthen a proposal. It covers matching on research topics, methods, publication records, and funding history. The goal is to form a team that can credibly deliver the proposed work and meet funder requirements. This activity sits within the broader grant development process, not the technical execution of AI research.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on public research databases, institutional directories, preprint servers, and grant databases. Many researchers use ORCID, Google Scholar, and university faculty pages to check publication records and current projects. Some funders provide partner search tools or matchmaking events. The site's own library of 135 research papers and 803 scientific models can serve as a source for identifying active work, but it does not link to the Consensus search tool.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first defining the scientific gap and the skills needed to close it. A researcher then searches literature and grant records for people who have published on adjacent problems or hold relevant datasets. Shortlisting involves checking co-authorship networks, citation patterns, and past funded projects. Outreach is usually direct, with a short note that names the specific paper or model that drew attention.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in collaborator finding center on data privacy, authorship expectations, and institutional conflict of interest rules. A researcher should not scrape personal contact details from restricted databases or share a candidate's unpublished work without permission. Early conversations should clarify who will lead, how credit will be assigned, and what each institution requires for grant submission. Provenance matters because a collaborator's prior work must be traceable to original papers, not to secondary summaries.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward more structured, machine-assisted matching across preprint servers, grant databases, and institutional profiles. Funders are experimenting with matchmaking platforms that use publication and funding history to suggest teams. The risk is that automated suggestions overvalue topical similarity and undervalue working style, trust, and complementary skills. Human judgment will remain central, but the search and screening steps will become faster.
